source: NCERT Class VIII, Curiosity: Textbook of Science, Ch. 11.

sections.heading: 1. Time and the Sky
points: People have measured time using **repeating events in the sky** — the **day** (Earth's rotation), the **month** (Moon's phases), and the **year** (Earth's revolution around the Sun).
The **day and night** result from the Earth's **rotation**; the **year** from its **revolution**.

sections.heading: 2. The Moon and the Month
points: The **Moon** revolves around the Earth; its changing shapes are the **phases of the Moon**.
One full cycle of phases (new moon → full moon → new moon) takes about **29.5 days** — the basis of the **lunar month**.
A **lunar calendar** is based on the Moon; a **solar calendar** on the Sun; India also uses **luni-solar** calendars.

sections.heading: 3. Ancient Timekeeping and Calendars
points: Early devices used the Sun and stars: the **sundial (shadow)**, and observing star positions.
**Calendars** organise days into weeks, months and years; the widely used **Gregorian calendar** has 365 days (366 in a **leap year**).
Indian traditional calendars (e.g. **Saka, Vikram Samvat**) and festivals often follow the Moon and Sun.

sections.heading: 4. High-Yield One-Liners (Last-Minute Recall)
points: Day = Earth's rotation; month = Moon's phases; year = Earth's revolution.
Lunar calendar (Moon) vs solar calendar (Sun); luni-solar combines both.
Sundial uses the Sun's shadow; Gregorian calendar = 365 days (366 in leap year).

sections.heading: 5. Common Traps (Watch Out)
points: A **lunar month** (Moon's phase cycle) is about **29.5 days**.
A **sundial** works only in the **daytime** using the Sun's shadow.
A **leap year** has **366 days** (an extra day in February).
